title: 6 NBA teams screwed over by the schedule release
description: The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in […]
fullText:
The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in 2023, reducing the number of division games and increasing interleague play to even things out.

The NBA does not play a balanced schedule, but the biggest factor in an individual team's success often feels like it has more to do with the travel arrangements than who they're playing on a particular night. Trimming the NBA's 82-game regular season schedule always felt like a silver bullet for many of the league's most pressing problems. Until that happens, teams are still jetting around the country every night to try to sell out as many arenas as possible.

The 2026-27 NBA schedule came out this week. Read our take on the league's 10 biggest rivalries for the upcoming season. With a little help from Shamit Dua's NBA Schedule Dash Board, these are the teams who got hit the hardest by the schedule makers this year.

The Celtics' 16 back-to-backs are in a five-way tie for the most in the NBA. They play 22 times in a stretch of three games in four nights, which ranks as the eighth hardest in the league. They are -4 in "net rest" games, which measures who the more tired opponent is in a given game. The Celtics aren't just dealing with the loss of Jaylen Brown this season, they're also needing to navigate one of the league's hardest travel schedules. I still think the Celtics will be a regular season wins machine, and I wouldn't count them out for grabbing the No. 1 seed in the East, but the road to get there looks more daunting after the schedule release.

The Pelicans have the hardest schedule in the NBA this year. New Orleans plays a league-leading 16 back-to-backs, they're the only team in the NBA with 27 'three in four nights' stretches, and they have a -5 net rest disadvantage. The Pelicans already had the league's seventh-lowest over/under at 29.5 wins coming into the season, and it feels like it's going to be an uphill climb to even hit that number. New head coach Jamahl Mosley has his work cut out for him. After years of believing in Zion Williamson, I'm finally giving up the dream that he can be one of the NBA's best players. At this point, I'm more interested in seeing what Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen can do together.

The Bulls are one of the league-leaders with 15 back-to-backs this season. They play a stretch of three games in four nights 24 times, which is the fourth most in the league. They're -3 on "net rest," which is third-hardest in the league. The Bulls also have five time zone crossings on no rest, which is the fifth-most in the league. The first 15 games of the season are especially brutal for Chicago, with two games against Boston, two games against the Knicks, two games against the Sixers, and one game each vs. San Antonio, Minnesota, and Cleveland. The Bulls are starting yet another rebuild, but it's going to be difficult for this fanbase to be patient when the team has the third worst cumulative record in the NBA after the last nine seasons. This year is more about figuring out if they have a future star in Caleb Wilson, and seeing how Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey develop in their third year together. The Bulls actually have a decent bench led by Leonard Miller, Jalen Smith, and Tre Jones, and they're going to need it with this type of schedule.

The Cavs missed out on LeBron James and got a tough schedule to boot. Cleveland is tied for the league-lead with 16 back-to-backs. They have 23 'three in four nights' games, which is the sixth hardest in the NBA. They're a -2 in rest advantage, also sixth hardest. The Cavs have done a whole lot of nothing this summer coming off the world's least convincing conference finals run, but there's still time to potentially land Peyton Watson or swing a big trade. I just get the sense that Cleveland's Eastern Conference rivals are passing them by … unless Evan Mobley has another leap left in him.

The Mavericks have 16 back-to-backs (tied for the most in the league), and they're at a -3 net rest advantage. It will be fascinating to see how Dallas manages Kyrie Irving as he returns from a torn ACL at age-34. The team will also have to manage Dereck Lively II, because the 22-year-old big man still hasn't been cleared to run after having foot surgery in December. I could see a world where Cooper Flagg takes a big leap and carries the Mavs to playoff contention, but it's important to remember Flagg won't turn 20 years old until just before Christmas. It might be wise for Dallas' new front office to take a more long-term view around their franchise star.

The Lakers play 15 back-to-backs. They face three games in four nights 26 times, which is the second most in the league. There's so much riding on Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves this year. Both of them dealt with injuries last year, playing 115 out of a possible 164 games. That's not going to cut it this year. Doncic and Reaves need to carry this offense every night without LeBron James around, and the Lakers probably don't want to know what happens when Quentin Grimes needs to be their first or second option for a night. Will the Lakers have a plan to save Luka in some back-to-backs? It's going to be a battle in the Western Conference every night, but the Lakers really just need him healthy for the playoffs, unlike last year.

title: Thurman Thomas & 34 Group, Inc. key to Bills’ new Highmark Stadium construction
description: NFL Hall of Fame RB Thurman Thomas, who played 12 seasons for the Buffalo Bills, weighs in about new Highmark Stadium and more.
fullText:
Thurman Thomas is a legend and an icon whose tenacity and grit coupled with truly awe-inspiring traits as a shifty dual-threat running back paved the way for an NFL Hall of Fame career that lasted 12 seasons with the Buffalo Bills. The franchise's Super Bowl teams were perhaps as much defined by Thomas' work as anyone else on the roster.

Teams simply weren't ever quite sure when or where Thomas was going to make them pay, what his next move was from play to play. Keeping up with Thurman Thomas proved far more difficult than anyone had predicted. That proved even more remarkable when years after his retirement Thomas revealed that he played his entire NFL career with a partially torn ACL in his left knee. That's sheer grit and determination, like few others then or now.

At a position with so much franchise star power through various generations, Thomas continues to rise above the rest. He was the complete package on the field then, and he remains so decades after having taken his last handoff in a Bills uniform. For a man who's now spent half his life in Western New York, it might be easy to look back and say he's done it all. Yet, if you ask Thomas, he'd likely tell you he's just getting started.

In a recent conversation with Thurman that set out intent on covering as much ground as was true of his tremendous career, we were drawn to the here and now. For at this moment, something special is unfolding for the whole of Bills Mafia. In case you haven't read the headlines or opened social media in some weeks, One Bills Drive has cut the ribbon on their new home, a completely new, from the ground up, version of Highmark Stadium.

In fact, the franchise just held its first public event for season ticket holders and other lucky fans of the team. In holding its annual "Return of the Blue & Red" practice, the Bills showed more than 50,000 die-hard supporters what all the fuss was about in that giant structure taking shape the last three years across Abbott Road.

Interestingly enough, that's where Thomas' connection here takes shape. While his jersey and number have been retired and adorn the inside of the new Highmark Stadium, that's not his only place of prominence within its walls. Truth be told, Thomas has his name displayed and honored in three separate places inside the new stadium, plus as part of the ring of honor outside the stadium's confines in what's known as the Family Circle.

Yet, the why and where of Thomas' name being included so many places isn't immediately obvious outside of his football career. In speaking with him, the story of a poignant full-circle moment unfolds that finds Thomas continually give back to the community that lifted him on its shoulders.

Thurman and his wife Patti Thomas established 34 Group, Inc. in Buffalo, NY in 2016. As a small business and commercial construction company, 34 Group is a "New York State Certified Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) providing design, construction management and self-performed construction services." Coincidentally, 34 Group was also one of the companies chosen to help with construction of the Bills' new stadium.

Thomas understands the challenges facing any startup, noting the necessary hill climb, and "to be an up-and-coming new group in the Buffalo area, it was a struggle at first." The company wasn't focused on the large prize at first, with Thomas saying "we were confident that we were going to be just a small company — just helping out, really. I mean, because, to have something like a stadium built, we couldn't handle that on our own. And that was Turner and Gilbane [joint venture construction management team Gilbane Building Company and Turner Construction Company] who led the charge for getting everybody set."

Even after this project, Thomas maintains that "we were just the little guys, you know, but we put in all 60 thousand of the seats in the new Highmark Stadium, courtesy of Irwin [Irwin Seating Company]. And they've done an outstanding job with us," while adding that 34 Group also "did some stuff for the grass field."

Focusing exclusively on commercial projects has allowed the Thomases and 34 Group to build a deeper connection with people in Buffalo. Thomas welcomes that bond, saying that it's been really helpful and "gotten me back into the community."

With that community comes projects of all sizes for 34 Group. "Yeah, sure, this was a $2.2 billion job for this stadium, but for our company — we take the $50,000 dollar jobs, we take the $100,000 dollar jobs. Thomas constantly strives to capture something beneficial in any endeavor, stating of a any potential project that "it's that relationship that I always tell my employees that we're not going to win every single job, but make sure you have a relationship, a communication person you can always talk to, because something's always going to pop up."

It's clear Thomas is happy diving into his work with 34 Group, saying that "it's been great, man. I love doing the work around here in the Buffalo area. Thomas maintains that 34 Group is about so much more than the next project. "I mean it's opened so many doors to where — not that we get work — but it's opened so many doors for other things, and I think that's the most important thing, besides our company, is the relationship that we have with the folks in the Buffalo area."

For Thomas, it's perhaps a passion project like no other yet, and one that fate helped connect to his prior career. In asking Thomas about the experience of working alongside other construction outfits and contractors, he said "it's been a really good experience for a lot of the companies in the Buffalo area because I think everybody got a piece of [the action] to do something. I think that was kind of the thing that when we [began building] this stadium — we wanted everybody to get a piece of it. Right? And I think everybody did."

Thomas humbly defers to the expertise and work of the tradespeople within 34 Group. Again, it's a team that undertook the installation of each and every seat — all 60,129 of those red and blue seats — in the new Highmark Stadium. It's an accomplishment he wears proudly upon his sleeve, and something that continues to fuel each and every return trip. "I've been over there probably five or six times in the last couple of weeks and they're still tweaking some things or whatever," Thomas said. A clear sign that despite the already finished look there is still much to do before the regular season is ushered in.

What stands out to him in speaking with folks around town is the sheer magnitude of the project. "From what I'm hearing, a lot of the positives are that people are saying: 'Is this really in Buffalo? Is this type of stadium really in Buffalo?,'" Thomas quipped. "To me, I think it's night and day when you talk about the old Highmark and you talk about the new Highmark. This one here, it's spectacular, there's a lot to see in there and there's a lot of room — a lot of space for the fans to walk around," he added.

Then in a nod to fans' obvious passion for new place, Thomas with a smile on his face said that it was evident during the Blue & Red practice that "everybody wanted to walk around the stadium, right, to see everything — instead of being in their seats." Honestly, who can blame them? Still, it's noteworthy when quarterback Josh Allen is upstaged in any stadium.

With any public project, critiques are bound to catch fire as soon as folks find something to latch onto, either first-hand or from afar. Thomas understands where some fans are coming from in terms of slight-line concerns, but he'd prefer to let the experts handle individual needs, while he focuses on the bigger picture. "It's an outstanding stadium, and I'm so proud that Buffalo does have this," Thomas said emphatically.

As for those seating concerns? Thomas knows it's not unique to Highmark Stadium, stating that "you can go around to all 32 teams in the National Football League, and you're going to have some type of obstructed view or whatever, not a good seat." At the same time, he understands well that people aren't getting the full picture of the situation on social media. "I've been telling people that those seats aren't really made for football. They're made for something else besides, like a concert or something like that," chalking up a lot of the concerns to people taking photos mostly from seats that won't be sold for Bills games.

For Thomas, the here and now is about the new stadium's positive aspects, which extends far beyond the tactile materials. "You know, obviously there's going to be some people out there that don't agree with certain things about the stadium," as nothing on Earth seems to earn unanimous accord simply because there are so many unique perspectives in society. But Thomas isn't ready to concede defeat, in the next breath wondering: "Are those people really fans? Are they really truly fans that are saying 'we're here to watch a football game. We're here to watch our team finally get over the hump to win a Super Bowl. That's all we're here for. I don't care about some obstructed view or anything like that.'"

Thomas continues focusing on the bigger picture, while allowing others to handle the concerns behind the scenes. "I'm sure the Bills and Gilbane and Turner, they'll take care of that situation, they'll do what they need to do in order to move forward. I don't like to hear the negativity talk. I'd like to hear positive talk going forward. We've got a really good football team with a really good chance to win a Super Bowl this year."

It's true that 34 Group is a huge focus for Thomas these days, but it's not his only focus. In a new partnership with Carhartt®, Thomas has found a clothing company that meets the demands of those tradespeople with 34 Group. It's also a company that understands what it means to be hard-working and blue collar. That's something the team has leaned into with its new alternate "Nickel City" uniform in homage to the people of Western New York.

None of that is lost on Thomas, who pointed out how great the new relationship is that he has with Carhartt®. "You know just a couple of years ago they called and wanted to do something with me, with my company at the new stadium. Well of course I don't have any pull over there to get that done so they actually had to call the Buffalo Bills and call the NFL to see if they can someway work something out and it's just one of those things that happened."

Thomas continues to deflect attention, praising the efforts made by both Carhartt® and One Bills Drive. "They worked it out, Carhartt®, you know, had given a lot of money to the community here in Buffalo, which I think they'll continue to do to have that relationship with the Bills, and have that relationship with my company. So, it has turned out great for us, they've been outstanding."

It takes a lot more than large companies to get the work done, however. With a project as grand as Highmark Stadium, that's where an authentically blue-collar attitude pays dividends. Thomas knows that well, especially as it relates to his team and those who have brought the new Highmark to life.

The new home of the Bills really feels like a place built for Buffalo by their neighbors. Thomas points out that the organization got things right in paying tribute to those who helped build a better Highmark. "I think it's on the east side of the stadium, they also have their names on the side of the building for everybody who worked there. It's all about the tradespeople. The ones that really do all the work," Thomas stated.

A dedicated team leader, Thomas understands his role and where he's able to make a positive impact on the team. "I'm not over there doing the work, you know what, but I want to encourage my employees and let everybody know that 'hey, you're doing a great job over here.'"

"It's really the people, the tradespeople that really make this stadium go, that got this stadium built. Without them, we wouldn't be here today. That stadium would not be done," Thomas said. "They've done an outstanding job and it's all about them, it's all about the tradespeople because day in and day out they were over there every single day, no matter what the weather was like, no matter what anything was like they were out there always ready and prepared to go."

These days when discussing the Bills, it seems as though all anyone can talk about is the new stadium. There are a lot of reasons to be excited for the 2026 season, with a new group of coaches in leadership positions, and of course Josh Allen and the rest of the team. However, Highmark Stadium's rebirth is going to demand attention.

The hype is real, and the Blue & Red event was only the tip of the iceberg. Saturday afternoon is the first preseason game on the new grounds, and the players are thrilled to have natural grass waiting for them.

But Saturday is as much about the fans. Even if it's only an exhibition game where the starters may or may not play a meaningful amount of snaps, it's an opportunity for Bills Mafia to test out their lungs.

To help get the crowd pumped, Thomas revealed a giveaway waiting for roughly a third of the first people to enter Highmark. "Saturday, the first 20,000 fans that enter the stadium will get this towel that has every single tradesperson's name on it," a clever rally towel serving as a nod to the hard work that brought the Bills' new home to life.

It will be difficult for anyone entering the new Highmark to forget just how many people were responsible for its development and construction. We've already seen photos of the steel girder adorned by signatures of those involved. There's also a section of wall that lists every person who helped with the stadium's construction, which includes Thomas' name. "Actually, my name is in that building three times," Thomas said. "So… out there on the wall as I said where all the workers (names) were. There's a beam where a lot of the companies signed, and obviously having my jersey retired, my number's in there with Jim and Bruce, and up there with Mr. Wilson also. So, yeah, I'm in there three times," Thomas proudly stated.

As for Saturday afternoon? "Definitely, they'll be pumped," Thomas exclaimed. Bills fans will get two preseason games at home to practice for the regular-season home opener in Week 2. Will waiting until Week 2 stunt the vibe due to a Week 1 road date against the Houston Texans? Thomas isn't convinced that's true, saying "I think, you know, even though with us opening up in Houston on Sunday and they're still playing a game Thursday (Week 2) the fans are like — because it's going to be a tough game in Houston with that defense — but win, lose, or draw, come that Thursday night, the opening of Highmark Stadium, it's going to be electric not only for Bills Mafia and the fans here, but I think when people are watching the game." With the game being in primetime, Thomas is certain that the new stadium's proper opening will resonate with viewers. "I'm sure there'll be some type of highlights where they're showing everybody the stadium, I can guarantee everybody's going to be like 'you know what, that's great for the Buffalo Bills. That's absolutely fantastic.'"

It's fair to say it feels a bit surreal that the stadium is now ready. Thomas summed it up well in saying "it's magical the way it's come together. It's nothing like the other Highmark. It's like, high-tech, red, white, and blue every seat, every place that you go, and it's absolutely gorgeous and I just… I know the people appreciate it." With a new state-of-the-art building for NFL football, you can bet fans will be ready to roar against opposing teams. For his part, Thurman's ready, excited for that moment. "I can't wait to really have it full on Thursday night against the Detroit Lions, you know it's going to be absolutely insane and… man, I'm ready to go. You know, as a Bills fan, you always say 'yeah, this is the year.' Yeah, I definitely think this is the year."

It's natural to guess that Thomas might have an affinity for James Cook, the Bills' current lead running back. Cook has been on an upward trajectory since being drafted 63rd overall by Buffalo during the 2022 NFL Draft. Thomas himself was also a second-round pick of the Bills, going 40th overall in the 1988 NFL Draft. There are plenty of professional similarities that allow them to bond, but their friendship runs far deeper than work parallels.

It's about family, and who Cook is as a person away from the football field. "James' been an outstanding guy. Ever since he got here, you know, we've been really good friends just because — and it's not because, yeah, he plays the position — but I look at his family, I look at his brother Dalvin Cook who I know very very well," Thomas mentioned.

They have a strong connection, Cook and Thomas. "He's such a nice guy; really doesn't say too much, but I think I'm one of those people who can really — I get a lot out of James Cook that anybody else normally wouldn't. So, it's a great relationship."

It's a relationship that allows Thomas to observe Cook's charitable efforts. Thomas knows as well as any former or current Bills player that what you do in the community says as much about you as your on-field effort. With Cook, Thomas sees his efforts as genuine and fruitful. "He's done a great job with the community work that he does," Thomas said.

Being a Buffalo Bill demands more of players than just their in-season work. "You know, you're here throughout the year. You know what? Help out the community," something that Thomas made strides to do as a player and continues doing now later in life. As for Cook's work in that realm? "He's done an excellent job. Really, that whole organization, all those player have done an excellent job of being in the community and doing things for Bills Mafia and people around there."

Many Bills fans have called for Cook to get more opportunities as a receiver, something Thomas did well during his career. Thomas agrees, and says that "hopefully that'll be coming," while revealing "I talked to him like, 'yeah, you know what, with your ability, and your speed, and your quickness, man, I really would like to see a little bit more out of you in the passing game.

There's more to Cook developing further as a receiver than just having plays called for him. He needs to continue working toward a full-time role where sometimes he isn't the focal point as a blocker instead, which Thomas isn't shy to point out. "In order for him to do that, he has to be out on the football field first, second, and third down. So, I don't know how much that's going to come into the offense, but I think he's ready to go and have an even better year this year."

While chatting with Thomas at the new stadium, Cook revealed that his personal goals this coming season are to try and win the NFL rushing title again, and to rush for 2,000 yards in the process. Of course, top of mind is his quest to help bring the Lombardi Trophy home to Orchard Park, NY next February.

Thurman Thomas continues to lead by example as an inspirational person who works to improve his community and help lift others up. Much of that is due to Patti and Thurman's charitable efforts, but also because they decided to invest in building Buffalo better.

In many ways, the new Highmark Stadium is a fitting tribute to the work done by so many Western New Yorkers on a daily basis. That includes those lofty heights Thomas, his teammates and coaches continually battled back against in pursuit of Super Bowl Glory.

At the end of the season, Thomas may be right in saying that this really is the Bills' year. Should that play out as true, then he and 34 Group, Inc. will have played a part in bringing Bills Mafia a whole new level of energy and life at home. It all has the feel of a story 30 years in the making.

title: Next Jordyn Tyson? Former Colorado WR hopes to follow same path at ASU
description: During his time in Tempe, Jordyn Tyson blossomed into a first-round NFL draft pick after coming from Colorado. Another ex-Buff wants to do the same.
fullText:
Hines Ward knows there is no replacing Jordyn Tyson.

Tyson is a one-of-one. After coming over from Colorado following a serious injury as a freshman, Tyson blossomed into a first-round NFL draft pick under the guidance of Ward as the wide receivers coach at Arizona State.

"You know, there'll never be another JT," Ward told The Arizona Republic at its annual trip to Payson for Camp Tontozona.

But there's no denying the connections that some will make with another former Colorado Buff now in the ASU receiver room: Omarion Miller. In the offseason, Miller made the move from Boulder to Tempe via the transfer portal, following the same path as Tyson in 2023.

While Ward said Tyson is a unique player, he sees similarities between the two.

"Both competitors. JT, he hates losing. He hates any DB covering him one time and talking trash to him. He wants to redo it right then and there. Similarities are the same. Always extremely competitive, wants to win every time. He wants to make sure he's in the right spot making plays. I try not to compare people. People have their own little style to them."

Echoing what he said about Tyson, Ward ended his answer with, "There'll probably never be another Omarion."

The connections between Miller and Tyson extend further. During his visit to Colorado, Miller was hosted by none other than Tyson.

When Tyson made the move to ASU, Miller kept tabs on him. While he was busy with his own season at Colorado, Miller couldn't help but notice how well Tyson was doing with the Sun Devils.

"I definitely watched him during our season, being that during that season he was one of the better receivers in that class, so I kept an eye on him," Miller told The Republic. "Happy for him, he's in the league doing what he can. Wish I would have got a chance to play with him."

Seeing what Ward and the coaching staff did with Tyson, turning him "into an overall receiver," is what drew Miller to the school.

"Once he came here, the three years, the development that I've seen him change from was eye-catching to me," Miller said.

Miller is coming off his best season yet at the college level, with 45 receptions for 808 yards and eight touchdowns in 2025. He was regarded as a four-star transfer prospect and was seen as one of the biggest additions of the offseason for ASU. Miller was named to the All-Big 12 preseason team for the upcoming season.

At 6-foot-2 and weighing 215 pounds, Miller's build is similar to Tyson (6-foot-2, 200). Miller has the speed to break away from defenders but can also take a hit across the middle of the field with his frame.

"Very elusive," Ward said. "For his size, to be able to move, to be able to run, to change direction, and then, of course, exceptional ball skills. Watching him when we played Colorado last year, it just stood out on tape. I'm extremely happy to work with somebody with his skill set. He's just an all-around football player. I'm giving him the blueprints. Hopefully, he can go out there and help win some games for us."

Miller has drawn the attention of coach Kenny Dillingham, who recently said at Camp T, "He's been great. He's pushed himself a lot this camp."

At this time last year, Miller said he viewed himself mainly as an "X" receiver, the position that lines up on the outside. But Miller now feels like he is an "all-around" wide receiver who can play anywhere on the field.

It's been part of Miller's growth, both on and off the field, after joining the Sun Devils.

"O's a special dude," offensive coordinator Marcus Arroyo said. "Obviously, we all know about the skill set, right? I think his best attributes are, probably, the person. That's the piece you don't know about when you go out and you're in the transfer portal. You try to do the best background you can. But until you fuse them into your culture, you really don't know what's going to take shape.

"And he is a beautiful human. Awesome young man. Loves to work on and off the field. Carries the standards, carries our identity as an offense and a culture to the utmost. He does all the skill set stuff we know about. He hasn't been very long, and he's totally committed to being part of our culture and our team that fast. That's exactly what you hope to get."

Ward said Miller has grown tremendously since coming to Tempe in January. Players gravitate toward Miller and he's already become a key piece of the locker room. A viral video in March of a Miller one-handed catch on a punt certainly helped.

Not a single snap has been played yet for 2026. But Ward has a way of looking ahead. Only a few months after being hired at ASU, Ward said about Tyson, "We haven't scratched the surface of how good he can really be as an individual and as a football player."

Ward feels similarly about Miller.

"His ceiling's so high, all the abilities there," Ward said. "He can play at the next level. Now, it's just honing in the good habits, understanding what it takes to get to that level, to take care of your body, to jump in the playbook, what you do on a daily basis, basically being a pro at it. He's learned, he's grown since January. But all I've seen is taking strides and taking steps forward."

Logan Stanley is a sports reporter with The Arizona Republic who primarily focuses on high school, college and Olympic sports. title: Fertility medication caused drug ban, says NFL player
description: Two-time Super Bowl winner Nazeeh Johnson believes he tested positive for a banned substance because of fertility medication he was taking.
fullText:
Two-time Super Bowl winner Nazeeh Johnson believes he tested positive for a banned substance because of fertility medication he was taking.

The Tennessee Titans cornerback has been suspended for six regular-season games without pay for violating the NFL's performance-enhancing substances policy.

The 28-year-old says that he and his wife have received fertility treatment after being told that he was infertile.

"I was not aware that there was a substance in the medication that was on the banned list and I tested positive for a PED [performance-enhancing drug]," he said on X., external

"Lesson to all NFL players and new players coming into the league: do not put anything in your body without following the process and getting approval beforehand.

"We lost our baby a few weeks ago, and this has been an incredibly difficult time for my wife and me. Fortunately, we have nine good eggs left, so we're holding on to hope that we'll be able to grow our family."

Johnson was drafted by the Kansas City Chiefs in 2022 and helped them win the Super Bowl in 2023 and 2024, before joining Tennessee in July.

He is eligible to participate in all pre-season activities, including games, before his suspension begins on 30 August.

The Titans' season opener is on 13 September and Johnson will be eligible for reinstatement on Monday, 19 October.

title: Bart Scott says ESPN chose worst possible time to tell him he lost his job
description: Ryan Clark headlined ESPN’s first round of summer layoffs because ESPN chose to inform him by pulling him off the air from NFL Live on July 20. Bart Scott was also part of the layoffs, but he flew relatively under the radar, even though ESPN apparently informed him in a similarly ruthless way. “Hey, man,…
fullText:
Ryan Clark headlined ESPN's first round of summer layoffs because ESPN chose to inform him by pulling him off the air from NFL Live on July 20. Bart Scott was also part of the layoffs, but he flew relatively under the radar, even though ESPN apparently informed him in a similarly ruthless way.

"Hey, man, I was going into my radio show, and they called me, like, 'Hey, uh, just to let you know, wish we could do it in person,'" Scott said while appearing on The Joint Venture Show with Craig Carton and Lil Wayne this week. "Like, no, you don't, motherf*cker. 'Oh, I wish I could do it in person!' Nah. So, it's like, 'We're not gonna renew you.' My contract is expiring in September. So, I found out that way."

Despite the lack of respect, Scott explained why he didn't let the nature of his exit tarnish his entire tenure or his outlook on his future.

"It's part of the business," Scott said. "You understand the balance, and I don't know what they had to do when they had to trim the fat. I had never been there, where my contract was expiring, because usually when it's a year, I get renewed. But it's what it is, man. Sometimes, losing your job can be some of the biggest blessings because it forces you to try and do something else and, sometimes, step out of your comfort zone.

"Listen, one thing that is constant is change, and I've been fired before. I understand the process, and I hold no ill will. I don't even know who made the call. But I did enjoy my time there. I enjoyed using the platform, keeping myself relevant. I wasn't a first-round draft pick; I'm not a Hall of Famer. I think I was a pretty good player, but I just appreciate them giving me the platform, and I'm not gonna hold any ill will toward them. It's my job to make them regret it."

Scott entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent, signing with the Baltimore Ravens in 2002. He became an impact linebacker with the Ravens (2002-08) and New York Jets (2009-2012). After retiring, Scott joined CBS Sports' NFL Today studio crew as an analyst. With Carton and Lil Wayne, Scott cited that experience as a precursor to understanding ESPN's decision to move on.

"I thought I was going to be able to work with Shannon [Sharpe]," Scott said. "But, sometimes, in this business — at least back then — they want shows to look a certain way."

"White?" Carton bluntly posited.

"Yeah, you can't have too many of us," Scott said. "Me and Shannon are similar. We represent a certain type of demographic. We're both funny, loud, loquacious, all that type of stuff, and I never got the opportunity."

Scott joined ESPN in a limited capacity on The Michael Kay Show on ESPN 98.7 in 2017, eventually becoming a full-time personality across ESPN platforms in 2020. He most recently co-hosted Bart & Carlin on ESPN New York and appeared on ESPN's Get Up! and First Take.

title: Commanders' Dorance Armstrong suspended for season opener vs. Eagles
description: Washington Commanders defensive end Dorance Armstrong receives a one-game suspension for violating the NFL's Personal Conduct Policy.
fullText:
Washington Commanders defensive end Dorance Armstrong has been suspended for the first game of the season for violating the NFL's Personal Conduct Policy. He will be eligible to participate in all preseason activities, including playing in Washington's preseason games.

His suspension begins on August 30, and he will be eligible for reinstatement on Mon. Sept. 14. This means he will miss Washington's season opener against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sun. Sept. 13. However, he will be available for the Commanders' game against the Dallas Cowboys on Sun. Sept. 20. Public records show that back in May of 2025, Armstrong was arrested in Frisco, Texas, for misdemeanor assault causing bodily injury as well as resisting arrest.

When Armstrong returns against the Cowboys in Week 2, it will be his first game since tearing his ACL against Dallas in Week 7 of last season. Prior to his torn ACL, Armstrong was having arguably the best season of his career with 5.5 sacks and seven tackles for loss in just seven games.

This year will be his third year with the Commanders and ninth season in the NFL. Armstrong spent the first six seasons of his career with Dallas, where he recorded a total of 23.5 sacks, 169 total tackles, and 48 quarterback hits. He has been a starter for most of his time with Washington and is expected to play a big role in the Commanders' defensive rotation this season.

title: Former Eagles Pass Rusher Eyes NFL Return After Unretirement Decision
description: One of the Philadelphia Eagles old friends has made an unexpected decision regarding his football future. The post Former Eagles Pass Rusher Eyes NFL Return After Unretirement Decision appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Eagles are entering what feels like a very important season in 2026. After a wild card exit in the playoffs last year, the Eagles need to make a deeper playoff run in order to keep their fans and the front office happy. While there's still a lot of work to be done between now and the start of the regular season, Philly has put together some solid work early on in training camp.

One of the team's biggest goals this offseason involved finding some help in the pass rush department, which led to the acquisition of Jonathan Greenard in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings. As folks will remember from last year, one of the team's top pass rushers, Za'Darius Smith, opted to retire from football early in the year, but after surprisingly deciding to unretire, he has taken a big step towards making his return to the NFL.

A fourth-round pick in the 2015 NFL Draft, Smith made a career for himself as a pass-rush specialist, spending time with several different teams. Along the way, he's earned three Pro Bowl selections and a spot on the All-Pro Second Team in 2020, which was the best season of his career (52 tackles, 12.5 sacks, two pass breakups, four forced fumbles).

Smith latched on with the Eagles right before the start of the 2025 campaign, but his usage patterns immediately raised concerns. While he picked up 10 tackles and 1.5 sacks in five games, Smith decided to retire in October, leaving Philadelphia in a tough spot when it came to finding players who could get after the quarterback.

The front office managed to address that need this offseason, but it will surely be intrigued to see that Smith is planning a return to the NFL. Reports emerged on Thursday afternoon indicating that, now that he has officially unretired, Smith is taking a free agent visit with one of his former teams, the Cleveland Browns.

"Free agent pass-rusher Za'Darius Smith, who recently un-retired with the possibility of playing, worked out for the Browns today," Ian Rapoport of NFL Network reported in a post on X.

GettyPhiladelphia Eagles edge rusher Za'Darius Smith.

Considering how Smith's time with the Eagles unfolded, he probably isn't remembered too fondly by fans, as he left the team in a tough spot when he decided to retire. That's just how the cookie crumbles sometimes, though, and with Greenard in tow now, you can make an argument that the pass rush is significantly improved (assuming he can stay healthy, of course).

There's no guarantee Smith will be returning to the NFL, but he seems intent on finding his way back ahead of the 2026 campaign. A return to the Eagles almost certainly will not happen, but several other teams are expected to show interest in him alongside the Browns, and given his ties to Philly, fans will likely be keeping close tabs on his status as he attempts to find his way back into the league.

title: NFL analyst Damien Woody joins list of ESPN on-air talent cuts
description: Former Pro Bowl offensive lineman Damien Woody, who won two Super Bowls with the New England Patriots, will not have his contract renewed at ESPN.
fullText:
Two-time Super Bowl champion Damien Woody is the latest high-profile on-air personality to be let go by ESPN.

Woody, whose contract was not renewed, joins the list of recent layoffs which includes Ryan Clark, Cam Newton and Karl Ravech.

Woody, 48, played 12 seasons in the NFL as an offensive lineman for the New England Patriots, Detroit Lions and New York Jets. He made the Pro Bowl in 2002 and won two Super Bowl rings with the Patriots.

"Still processing it all but I want to thank all of my colleagues at ESPN who made it a joy to talk ball for 15 yrs," Woody wrote in a post on X. "Being a guy who had a serious speech impediment to working on tv was truly one of my proudest accomplishments. Looking forward to what God has in store for me next!"

Woody was a regular on a number of ESPN shows over the years, including "Get Up," "Fantasy Football Now" and "First Take." He also frequently appeared as an NFL analyst on "SportsCenter."

According to The Athletic, ESPN executives informed Woody of the decision a few weeks ago. He will continue to appear on the air through the end of the month.

title: NBA on NBC schedules first ever Presidents Day quadrupleheader
description: Christmas Day has been the traditional home for the NBA’s marquee regular season showcase event. And in a brand new move, one of those holidays just happens to be the day after Super Bowl LXI. NBC has…
fullText:
Christmas Day has been the traditional home for the NBA's marquee regular season showcase event. But with the NFL now encroaching on their territory, the league is expanding its offering on other holidays.

And in a brand new move, one of those holidays just happens to be the day after Super Bowl LXI.

NBC has announced that the network will all four games for the first-ever Presidents Day quadrupleheader on February 15, 2027.

The lineup is headlined by some of the teams that the NBA will showcase on Christmas Day and Opening Night, but with some intriguing storylines added in.

It starts with LaMelo Ball and the Timberwolves visiting Charlotte in his first visit back to his former home. Then, LeBron James is featured once again, this time against former teammate Kyrie Irving, Cooper Flagg, and the Mavericks. The mouth-watering matchup between Victor Wembanyama and Giannis Antetokounmpo is the feature attraction at 5 p.m. ET with the Spurs facing the Heat. Finally, the nightcap will see the Indiana Pacers play the Golden State Warriors with a duel of Tyrese Haliburton and Steph Curry.

It's a forward thinking move from the NBA. Why not go all-in on a holiday that can literally take the ball from the NFL the day after the Super Bowl? It also helps that it's the middle of winter and lots of people throughout the country will be inside.

Additionally, NBC will have the Martin Luther King Jr. Day quadruple-header that has seen more emphasis from the NBA in recent years. That full lineup consists of Pistons-Cavs, Sixers-Hawks, Timberwolves-Knicks, and Rockets-Grizzlies. It's no coincidence that the only team to feature on all four premier national showcase occasions is LeBron James and the new-look Philadelphia 76ers.

For both doubleheaders, NBC and Peacock will carry games at 12 p.m. ET, 2:30 p.m. ET, and 5 p.m. ET. The last game in both sets will be at 7:30 p.m. ET and feature mainly on Peacock, but will also on linear television through NBCSN.

title: Former NFL QB Matt Hasselbeck part of latest CTE frontier — diagnosing brain disease in the living
description: Former NFL quarterback Matt Hasselbeck has participated in a study at Boston University to find ways to diagnose chronic traumatic encephalopathy in living individuals.
fullText:
Matt Hasselbeck took some nasty hits to the head during his 17-year NFL career, four years at Boston College and a childhood full of sports, but the quarterback seems to have emerged from more than two decades of collisions relatively unscathed, enjoying middle adulthood with his wife and three children.

The 50-year-old knows that some of his friends and former teammates haven't been as lucky.

That's why the three-time Pro Bowl selection recently spent two days at Boston University, going through a battery of scans and tests to determine how much all those collisions affected his brain. The hope is that it will be a small step toward a goal that has eluded doctors — diagnosing chronic traumatic encephalopathy in the living.

"They need guys like me — they need people who are feeling good to step up to the plate and volunteer," Hasselbeck said. "I played quarterback, so I didn't take some of the hits that a lot of my teammates took.

"But the guys who were blocking for me, or playing special teams, or trying to get the ball back for me on defense, I wanted to do something. They had my back, so in a way I'd like to have their back."

A degenerative brain disease that has been linked to concussions and other head trauma common in military combat and contact sports, CTE has been diagnosed in more than 100 former NFL players, casting a pall over the United States' most popular sports league. Some high-profile football players diagnosed with CTE after their deaths include Hall of Famers like linebacker Junior Seau and quarterback Ken Stabler, along with former Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez.

Right now, CTE can only be diagnosed after death.

CTE can affect regions of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions. This can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other cognitive and behavioral issues, though researchers note these symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses.

Hasselbeck's participation is just a small part of a study that Michael Alosco, co-director of clinical research at the Boston University CTE Center, hopes will expand to hundreds of participants in multiple locations. Alosco is the principal investigator in Boston and there are also sites in California, Arizona, Texas and Florida with potentially more to come.

The study seeks two types of people: Those who played professional or college football and those who have been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and never played contact or collision sports and have no history of repetitive head impacts.

Alosco said there are many similarities between Alzheimer's and CTE because both are degenerative brain diseases, but there are also some key differences, and mapping out those discrepancies is key to figuring out a way to diagnose CTE properly.

"We've applied what we've known worked for Alzheimer's disease, but we've learned it does not work for CTE," Alosco said. "We've really got to push discovery efforts and find the marker that's specific to the protein of CTE versus Alzheimer's because they're different.

"How we're going to get there is through the research we're doing right now."

Nicholas Ashton, the principal investigator in Phoenix, said roughly 10 patients have participated at the Arizona site. He said that currently, diagnosing CTE in the living is mostly guesswork because so many of the symptoms mimic Alzheimer's.

"The more people involved, the more information we get and the closer we get to an answer," Ashton said. "Treatments exploded with Alzheimer's once we were able to accurately diagnose. We're trying to get to the same spot with CTE."

Hasselbeck said he went through a variety of mental tests — like counting backward from 100 by sevens and reciting the alphabet backward. He also had a blood sample taken, an MRI on his brain and a PET (positron emission tomography) scan that injects a small amount of safe radioactive tracer that maps out the brain's function.

The former quarterback said the procedures were eye-opening and humbling.

"I've got a healthy respect for people who are dealing with serious brain trauma, whether it's tumors or cancer," Hasselbeck said. "I walked in there feeling completely healthy and you still get a little anxious when you're doing a brain scan, an MRI. You come out and you're looking at your brain."

Hasselbeck is also donating his brain for research after he dies.

Not everyone in the study is a famous former NFL player.

Bryan Savage, a 56-year-old who lives in Maryland, is a former linebacker at Union College in Schenectady, New York — an NCAA Division III school. He traveled to Boston for the study and also has committed to donating his brain.

Savage said he's lucky to be relatively healthy but that he's been diagnosed with depression and ADHD over the past few years.

"I was interested because of some of the things that I've gone through physically and mentally," Savage said. "You wonder if it's just getting older, a midlife crisis or if it's related to any brain trauma I might have had playing football."

Savage praised the researchers who were with him during the study and said he was relieved to find out his brain scans look normal for a man in his mid-50s. He's reached out to some of his former teammates, encouraging them to get involved in the study.

"I'll talk to some of my former friends and they're going through a lot of the same things," Savage said. "They'll say — 'Why do I feel like this? I've never been depressed. Things that I used to be passionate about I don't care about anymore.'"

Alosco said the main reason Alzheimer's research is much more advanced than CTE research is sheer numbers: Alzheimer's research dates back decades and there have been countless people who have been studied.

"The (Alzheimer's progress) is through years and years of research, of people donating their brains, and also collecting data during life," Alosco said. "While we've been studying CTE for a while, we haven't had the point where we've had all this data during life, that have also donated their brain. We need to get to that place."

He added: "I'm really hopeful about detecting CTE — I don't think that's too distant. Once we can accurately diagnose, that's when we can start some treatment trials."

Hasselbeck — who played in the NFL for the Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Tennessee Titans and Indianapolis Colts — said he had three concussions before he even started college, one playing football, another on the basketball court and another while goofing around while ice skating. He had a few concussions during his college or NFL career, but he wasn't sure of the exact number because some might have gone undetected since there was a culture of toughness in locker rooms, particularly early in his career.

Hasselbeck's pro career spanned from 1998 to 2015 and the quarterback said there was a huge change regarding head injuries during that time. Early in his career, the only acceptable answer after a hit to the head was "I'm good," but by the mid 2010s, players were much more honest about potential concussions.

Hasselbeck's proud of that change. Now he hopes his participation in the current CTE study can continue that progress.

"I've always had a passion for making the game safer," Hasselbeck said. "I love football. One of the things I'm most proud of as an NFL guy is not just as a player, but the entire time I worked with the league and NFLPA for ways to make the game safer."

title: Aaron Rodgers wanted to play at Lambeau field one last time
description: Future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers played the vast majority of his games throughout his NFL career at Lambeau Field as a member of the Green Bay Packers. Now, as he enters the final season of his storied career, he’ll never have a chance to play there again, and it sounds like he’s a…
fullText:
Future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers played the vast majority of his games throughout his NFL career at Lambeau Field as a member of the Green Bay Packers. Now, as he enters the final season of his storied career, he'll never have a chance to play there again, and it sounds like he's a little sad about it.

During a recent interview, Rodgers lamented the fact that Thursday night's preseason game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Packers is not at Lambeau Field, which would have given him one last time to play at the stadium where he played his home games for 18 seasons.

During a Zoom call with Packers reporters on Wednesday, Rodgers admitted that he wishes the upcoming preseason game had been scheduled as a road contest rather than a home game, even though returning as a visiting player would have been "strange."

"100%, 100%," Rodgers said via ESPN. "When I heard it was possible to play both my former teams, I was really hoping this one was going to be in Green Bay, not just to get back at Lambeau one more time, but to head out to Chives [restaurant] for a dinner and maybe head out to Green Bay Country Club for a quick nine or something. I was really hoping it was going to be in Green Bay for a lot of reasons.

"It would have been strange, being in that [visitors] locker room and stuff, but I would have found my way over, like many former players have over the years … and see some of the guys and see some of the trainers and equipment staff and all the people I really care about that still work there. Yeah, I was definitely bummed out that we weren't in Lambeau for this one."

While Rodgers no longer plays for the Packers, his message for the team, the city, the organization, and the fans was clear.

Asked what he will miss the most when he is retired, Rodgers said: "Definitely the people I got to do it with." And that included Green Bay.

"That's what this game's all about," Rodgers added. "It's about the relationships, and I'm just most thankful for all the men and women, you know, who've been in my life through this game over the years. So many great people in Green Bay, in the entire organization, top to bottom. You know, just salt of the earth type of people. … But the thing that actually lasts the longest is those people that impact your life, and there's been a lot of those, a lot especially in Green Bay, it had a huge impact on my life. So I think about those people a lot."

title: Former Washington football star returns to NFL training camp
description: After dealing with a knee injury, former UW star Jalen McMillan made his return to training camp on Tuesday.
fullText:

title: Briton Obada retires from NFL to pursue 'true calling'
description: After growing up in foster care, Efe Obada spent 10 years as an NFL player yet only now, on his retirement, does he feel he has found his "life's purpose".
fullText:
Efe Obada spent 10 years as an NFL player yet only now does he feel he has found his true calling.

After spending the 2025 season without a team, the 34-year-old Briton officially confirmed his retirement on Wednesday.

And to coincide with the announcement, Obada has launched his own foundation, which will help care-experienced people aged between 11 and 25.

"It resonates with me so much because I've lived it," he tells BBC Sport. "I know about the barriers, the isolation."

Obada lived in more than 10 foster homes after being trafficked from the Netherlands and abandoned in London at the age of 10.

He went on to make a remarkable journey to the NFL, where his career earnings were more than $8m (£6m).

"I now have the means and resources to have real impact on something that I hold very dear," he added. "It's everything to me. I feel like it's my life's purpose."

Obada was born in Nigeria and lived with his father before being trafficked to the Netherlands to reunite with his mother.

He and his sister, who was 11 and has learning difficulties, were then taken to the UK by a stranger who left them on a street in east London.

They ended up in the care of social services, who kept Obada and his sister together and placed them with black families in south London. In the worst of those situations, he has said they were treated like domestic slaves.

Obada managed to progress at school and college, and wanted to study architecture at university, but his progress was blocked because he was still classed as an illegal immigrant.

"I was an undocumented person so I couldn't go to university, couldn't get a career," he says. "It had to be cash-in-hand jobs. My life was going a certain direction."

As Obada sought a sense of belonging, he began mixing with the wrong crowd and lived with "some undesirable people".

"I was living in such dysfunction and toxicity, and everybody around me was too," he says. "It was just chaos and survival. And I didn't recognise that until I started sharing my life with people from different walks of life.

"They were like, 'oh, that's a bit messed up, you know'. So I started taking stock and realised that maybe I am worth more, maybe I do deserve better."

'Growing up in foster care translates to NFL'

At 22, Obada and his now wife had moved out of the city and he was working as a warehouse security guard.

From there, he says there was more chance of him "winning the lottery three times and getting hit by lightning four times" than making it to the NFL.

He bumped into an old friend who was playing American football for the London Warriors and invited Obada to come along.

After just five games at amateur level, one of the Warriors' coaches - future Super Bowl winner Aden Durde - helped secure a try-out with the Dallas Cowboys and Obada joined their practice squad in 2015.

He spent time with two other teams and "poured all his anger" into making it. When the defensive end earned his NFL debut with the Carolina Panthers in 2018, he had an instant impact - claiming a sack, an interception and forcing a fumble.

"That really put me on the map," he says. "There was a lot of pent-up frustration from all the rejections that led to that moment.

"Then playing for the Panthers in London in 2019 was a dream come true, to play in front of my friends and family on home soil, to show everybody what I'd been working towards."

Obada went on to play for the Buffalo Bills and Washington Commanders, racking up 80 games and 15 quarterback sacks, tackling the likes of Super Bowl winners Tom Brady, Aaron Rodgers, Drew Brees, Matt Stafford and Jalen Hurts.

"I didn't get [Patrick] Mahomes or Lamar [Jackson], they were two that I really wanted to, but that list is alright," he jokes.

Obada never reached a Super Bowl and has wondered might have been in the 2021 season, when his Buffalo team lost an epic play-off game against Mahomes' Kansas City Chiefs in overtime.

Obada was also on Washington's practice squad when they went within one win of the big game in 2025.

Obada has raised awareness of the care system and human trafficking throughout his career, while dealing with his own demons.

"I've managed to face the majority of it," he says. "It's taken time and been a learning curve, but the NFL, my marriage and the people I surround myself with has been instrumental in helping me grow out of that.

"I think I'm so far removed from who I was, being in that fight-or-flight mode. Now I can be my true authentic self and enjoy living my life.

"I have so much to give, and when I help my community, I just come to life because I can have real impact."

Obada, who finally became a British citizen last year,, external is now back in south London and will continue helping community projects and working in broadcasting.

But his focus will be establishing his foundation, which aims to provide a wide range of support services and, ultimately, a permanent community hub in south London.

"American football was my golden ticket, my way out," he says. "Playing in the NFL changed my life. It gave me a platform and the ability to provide.

"But I think this is my true calling. I want to create something that lasts, that matters. I want to support kids that are still in those situations and make sure they understand that their past doesn't define their future, that they can write their lives in the same way I did.

"Whatever their dream is, it's possible. When I was that age I was scared to dream, so helping them is nice, and it's something I'm going to continue until my money runs out!"

title: ‘It pissed him off’: New Eagles freak vows to show NFL teams what they ‘missed out on’
description: Eagles defender is motivated by offseason disrespect: "It pissed him off.'
fullText:
PHILADELPHIA — After being introduced as UTSA's cornerbacks coach in 2020, Nick Graham was told by another coach on the staff to watch Riq Woolen's tape from his first few practices at cornerback from the year before.

On that day, Graham discovered the best cornerback talent he had ever seen as a coach. Woolen had practiced as a cornerback for only one week during the 2019 season. He was still listed as a wide receiver on UTSA's roster.

Right away, Graham was enamored by Woolen's size (6-foot-4, 210 pounds), his elite speed and smooth hips. Not long after watching Woolen's film for the first time, Graham convinced Woolen to switch from wide receiver to cornerback.

"I go watch this tape and go, 'Whoa, God, I don't know what I did to deserve this, but thank you,'" Graham told NJ.com last week.

Graham is confident the Eagles will be thanking the rest of the NFL for allowing them to sign Woolen to a one-year, $12 million contract on March 10.

The Eagles are listed at +215 to win over 11.5 regular season games next season on DraftKings. Our complete DraftKings Sportsbook review provides a useful guide on how to navigate their app. Also, make sure to view our Eagles win total prediction for next season for a full expert breakdown.

Woolen, who was drafted by the Seattle Seahawks in the fifth round, was one of the NFL's best rookies in 2022, and over the last four years, he has proven to be one of the NFL's most talented cornerbacks. However, Woolen has not always been consistent, and that has gotten him into trouble.

Still, the way Graham sees it, Woolen is on the verge of a breakout.

"I think the Eagles got a steal, and I think they know it. I know they know it," Graham said.

Woolen's signing also carried personal meaning for Graham, whose own playing career began with the Eagles. Graham played his rookie season for the Eagles in 2007 as a backup cornerback and special-teams contributor. He knows what it's like to play in Philadelphia, and he is confident Woolen is a perfect fit.

"I texted Riq, 'I know you're (expletive) lying,'" Graham said about his reaction to the Eagles signing Woolen. "That was the first thing I said to him. He was like, 'Coach Graham, can you believe it? Can you believe I'm playing where you used to play?' I was just excited for him because I know the type of organization [the Eagles are]. I know the defense that is there. Man, I'm just excited for the kid. I really am."

Graham's excitement has not worn off since. He was shocked the Eagles were able to add Woolen to one of the NFL's best secondaries.

Woolen is receiving a fresh start with the Eagles, and Graham believes a change of scenery will unlock Woolen's talent.

The Seahawks benched Woolen multiple times over the last three years. He played 817 defensive snaps last year, the fewest of his career.

"He's not a finished product, but I believe he has gold jacket ability," Graham said.

Woolen, 27, has made one Pro Bowl, but Graham believes he can become a Hall of Fame-caliber player.

"Athletically, he's there, but just knowledge of the game and just mastering his technique and his craft, I don't think that he's there yet," Graham said. "And I think that when he puts that all together, I just don't know [if there is anyone better]. There may be three in the league that I could say, 'Oh, yeah, they're better.'

"And so, I just think that he has a rare skill set. I can go another 20 years, and I'll never coach an athlete like that. When he puts that all together, I think it's going to be scary hours."

It took some convincing, but Woolen is glad he was receptive to Graham's advice to play cornerback.

"I feel like it helped make me be the person I am today, and it shows that I can go through adversity, go through a whole position change and still become great," Woolen told NJ.com after Monday's training camp practice.

Woolen dealt with a shoulder injury in 2023 and was benched for a Week 15 game against the Eagles that year. He was also benched in 2024 for the opening drive against the Minnesota Vikings after violating undisclosed team rules.

Last season, Woolen drew a taunting penalty in the NFC Championship Game that nearly proved costly. On the next play, Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua beat him for a 34-yard touchdown, cutting Los Angeles' deficit to four points at 31-27.

But Woolen will not let those tough moments define him.

"Whenever you're making progress, it's like a roller coaster," Woolen said. "It's loops in all different ways, but you still gotta ascend. As long as you are still ascending, then you're doing the right things."

Despite being one of the best young talents available this offseason, Woolen received no long-term offers in free agency.

According to Next Gen Stats, Woolen allowed only 0.5 yards per coverage snap in man coverage, the lowest among outside cornerbacks. He also allowed a 31.3% completion rate in man coverage, the lowest among cornerbacks.

"I guarantee you it pissed him off," Graham said about Woolen not landing a big deal. "To me, he's a $20 million a year guy talent-wise."

Woolen admitted that not receiving big offers gives him extra motivation, but he's happy to be in a place where his career could take off.

"My whole thing is just getting everything down, being a great teammate, showing these guys that they can ride with me and be consistent," Woolen said. "Whenever the season comes, every week, I'll get my chance to prove to everybody else what they missed out on."

Graham doesn't think Seattle was the best place to develop Woolen.

"Going in and out like he was doing last year, nobody wants to do that," Graham said about Woolen rotating with Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe last year. "I don't think he's that type of player that needs to be doing that. And so, he's always confident, but I just think it's the love you receive. We're all humans. We want to be somewhere where we know that people care about us."

Woolen's new Eagles teammates and coaches have spoken highly of his abilities. Woolen will start this season across from All-Pro Quinyon Mitchell.

"To be here and to know that I have a role and I have a role that plays a big part in this team, it's a blessing for real," Woolen said. "Because that's something that I want, and that's something that I will excel at."

Woolen is best as a man-coverage cornerback, and the Eagles play more man coverage than Seattle does. Last year, the Eagles played man coverage on 24.5% of their snaps, while Seattle did so on 15.2%, according to Sharp Football Analysis.

Although Graham believes that Woolen will be targeted the most among the Eagles' cornerbacks, he expects Woolen to prove he is a top player at the position.

To Graham, nobody deserves that success more.

"He's the nicest kid ever, man," Graham said. "He loves his family, Got a great mama, great brother and sister. He just takes care of everybody. And he's the same person every day. There ain't a vindictive bone in his body. He's a good kid. He's always a pleasure to be around. Every time we talk, it's 'I love you.' I mean it, and I know that he means it. And so me and that kid will always have a special bond."

fullText:
The Minnesota Vikings worked out former Detroit Lions running back Jermar Jefferson. This was reported by the NFL's daily transaction wire on Monday afternoon.

Jefferson was originally drafted by the Lions in the seventh round of the 2021 NFL draft. He spent most of his time with the Lions between the active roster and the practice squad. Over the course of his career, he has also played with the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals. Both of those came last season. He was able to make a minor impact with the Cardinals, appearing in two games on special teams.

Jefferson has recorded 21 rushing attempts for 96 yards and two touchdowns. The playmaker has also tallied five receptions for 33 yards. Now, the Vikings brought him in to see if he could add to their strong running back room.

Jefferson had a successful college career. He played for the Oregon State Beavers from 2018 to 2020. Jefferson began his career strong, appearing in 12 games for the Beavers in 2018. He recorded 239 carries for 1,380 yards and 12 touchdowns. This included 254 rushing yards against Arizona State. Jefferson was named the Pac-12 Freshman Offensive Player of the Year for his efforts.

2020 was another season in which he was able to showcase his talents. His junior season saw him record 143 rushing yards per game and 6.5 yards per carry. All told, he tallied 133 carries for 858 yards and six touchdowns in six games. Jefferson was named the Co-Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Year and received first-team All-Pac-12 honors.

The proof of Jefferson's skill set was in the games he played. He had 1500-yard rushing games over 27 career appearances. It was easy to see why NFL teams wanted to take a chance on him.

The 2026 calendar year has been busy for him. He was signed by the San Francisco 49ers on May 28 to a one-year contract. He was waived just five days later on June 2. Jefferson also had a workout with the Green Bay Packers on July 27. This was a depth move on the part of the Packers as well. They were also able to see if he could help their team.

Now, the Vikings brought in Jefferson. The running back position is an interesting one for the Vikings, as Aaron Jones undoubtedly leads the way. Jordan Mason and Demond Claiborne also provide support. Claiborne in particular has had an intriguing training camp. The rookie has emerged as a pleasant surprise at the position, and could factor in heavily to the rotation sooner rather than later. The emergence of Claiborne has made it so running back depth is necessarily the most pressing need.

With that being said, it is never a bad thing to try and check off boxes and add players for depth purposes. This is exactly what the preseason is all about. If anything, the Vikings are doing a little bit of homework with their first preseason game on Thursday.

The offense has a chance to be explosive in the fall, and adding additional depth may be what is needed to get over the hump.

title: Four-Time NFL Pro Bowler Praises Dave Roberts Gesture Before Dodgers Game

fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers draw out celebrities for literally every home game. That included a past four-time Pro Bowler in the NFL Monday. Yet former Las Vegas Raiders and New Orleans Saints quarterback Derek Carr couldn't help but praise a kind gesture manager Dave Roberts made.

title: Mayobridge to Madden – Smyth enjoying next level in NFL
description: As he enters his first pre-season as an NFL starter, County Down's Charlie Smyth says he is getting used to being a player rather than fan of the sport.
fullText:
Entering just his third pre-season training camp with New Orleans, Charlie Smyth can hardly be dubbed a veteran at this stage of his fledgling NFL career but the Saints' incumbent kicker certainly no longer feels a novice either.

Smyth's big chance with the Saints came last November when he stepped up to replace a struggling Blake Grupe in Week 13 against the Miami Dolphins.

Signed to a three-year contract the following month, Smyth played in the final six games of the Saints' campaign, completing 12 of 16 field goal attempts and going a perfect on 13 extra-point attempts.

"I've got the experience in games to fall back on now," said the County Down native, who came through the league's International Player Pathway.

"It's been great to be into my third camp and feel a little more experienced, nothing here is foreign to me anymore.

"I've known the same special teams coordinator all my time here and he's been great with me.

"When you gain those relationships, it becomes familiar and I really do feel the support of everybody here. It's a cool feeling knowing that people want you to do well."

The raised profile of being an NFL starter still takes some getting used to - for instance, being the subject of fantasy football debates and seeing himself featured in the Madden computer game series.

"I remember one week, the game against the Jets where I scored five field goals and I think I scored something like 19 fantasy points, someone sent me a message or tweet pointing out that I'd scored more that week than Josh Allen, Travis Kelce, Jackson Dart etc and it was captioned 'This is why we love fantasy football!' – it was pretty funny.

"Then I saw myself in Madden there and thought this is mental. I used to play this game as a teenager growing up and I never thought I would be in that position.

"I am not getting carried away and am focused on being the player not the fan. I think I am doing a good job of that."

The GAA Social with Charlie Smyth

'Here we go' - what's it like to make your NFL debut?

During the off-season Smyth was able to compare notes with another Irish sportsman living stateside, the golfer Shane Lowry.

The pair spent time together at the Zurich Classic, a PGA Tour event in New Orleans, and aside from some good-natured GAA banter about the fortunes of their respective counties Down and Offaly, there was also a constructive discussion about the crossover between their two professions.

"Shane was brilliant. I walked the last couple of holes with him, I got to spend three or four hours with him," Smyth said.

"There are a lot of similarities between kicking and golf. From weight transfer to ball contact, hitting a draw or fade. We talked about the mentality of what he's thinking pre-shot, what I'm thinking pre-kick and we mashed it up.

"It was just a privilege to get to meet him."

For Smyth this camp brings the unfamiliar situation of looking over his shoulder at those eyeing his starting spot. This summer the Saints have added Tanner Brown, a UFL championship winner this year with the Louisville Kings, to their roster to vie with Smyth in the pre-season.

"It's just the way it is in this business. You don't take anything personally," he said.

"I've obviously been in this position with Blake in the past two off-seasons and even last year going in competition when the job was up for grabs.

"All the specialists are with each other all the time, it's the nature of the business. You just go out and execute to the best of your ability."
